If you have been injured in a car accident, the concept of "negligence" will be central to your claim. But not all negligence is equal under the law. The difference between ordinary negligence and gross negligence can dramatically affect the type and amount of compensation you recover — including whether punitive damages come into play. Understanding how Georgia and South Carolina courts distinguish between these two standards of fault is essential for anyone pursuing a personal injury claim after a crash.

before:
Gross negligence goes beyond a simple failure to use reasonable care. It represents a conscious and voluntary disregard of the need to use reasonable care, which is likely to cause foreseeable grave injury or harm to persons, property, or both. Gross negligence is sometimes described as conduct that shows a "reckless disregard" for the safety of others — the at-fault party knew or should have known that their behavior created a substantial risk of serious harm and proceeded anyway.

The distinction matters because gross negligence can unlock additional legal remedies that are not available in ordinary negligence claims, most notably punitive damages. It can also affect immunity protections, caps on damages, and the application of certain legal defenses.
after:
Gross negligence goes beyond a simple failure to use reasonable care. In Georgia it is the absence of slight diligence, "that degree of care which every man of common sense, however inattentive he may be, exercises under the same or similar circumstances" (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-4). South Carolina defines it as "the intentional conscious failure to do something which it is incumbent upon one to do or the doing of a thing intentionally that one ought not to do" (Etheredge v. Richland School District One, 341 S.C. 307 (2000)). Gross negligence is sometimes described as conduct that shows a "reckless disregard" for the safety of others — the at-fault party knew or should have known that their behavior created a substantial risk of serious harm and proceeded anyway.

The distinction matters because the aggravated conduct that makes negligence gross is often the same evidence that supports punitive damages, but gross negligence by itself is not enough in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b)), and South Carolina requires wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D)). In South Carolina it can also decide whether a government entity is immune (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(25)).

before: Georgia law explicitly recognizes three degrees of negligence under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-4: slight negligence (failure to exercise extraordinary care), ordinary negligence (failure to exercise ordinary care), and gross negligence (failure to exercise even slight care). This three-tier framework gives Georgia courts a structured approach to evaluating fault severity.
after: Georgia law explicitly recognizes three degrees of negligence under O.C.G.A. §§ 51-1-2 through 51-1-4: slight negligence (failure to exercise extraordinary care), ordinary negligence (failure to exercise ordinary care), and gross negligence (failure to exercise even slight care). This three-tier framework gives Georgia courts a structured approach to evaluating fault severity.

before: Georgia allows punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 when the defendant's conduct shows "willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression, or that entire want of care which would raise the presumption of conscious indifference to consequences." This standard effectively requires proof of gross negligence or worse. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases, though the cap does not apply when the defendant acted with the specific intent to cause harm or was under the influence of alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)(1)).
after: Georgia allows punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b) only on clear and convincing evidence that the defendant's conduct shows "willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression, or that entire want of care which would raise the presumption of conscious indifference to consequences." This standard requires more than gross negligence: the Supreme Court of Georgia has held that negligence, even gross negligence, will not support punitive damages (Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown, 258 Ga. 115 (1988)). Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (§ 51-12-5.1(g)), though the cap does not apply in product liability cases (§ 51-12-5.1(e)) or, against the active tort-feasor only, when the defendant acted with the specific intent to cause harm or while under the influence of alcohol or drugs to the degree that their judgment was substantially impaired (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)).

before: South Carolina courts define gross negligence as the failure to exercise slight care — essentially the same concept as Georgia's framework. The South Carolina Supreme Court has described gross negligence as "the failure to exercise the degree of care which even the most careless person would exercise." This standard applies across all personal injury claims, including wrongful death cases and premises liability claims.
after: South Carolina courts define gross negligence as the failure to exercise slight care — essentially the same concept as Georgia's framework. Etheredge, quoting Clyburn v. Sumter County School District Seventeen, 317 S.C. 50 (1994), puts it plainly: "It is the failure to exercise slight care." The same definition applies whenever gross negligence is at issue, including in wrongful death cases and premises liability claims, and it is the threshold for suing a government entity over how it supervised a student, patient or prisoner (§ 15-78-60(25)).

before: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D), South Carolina allows punitive damages only where the plaintiff proves that the harm was the result of the defendant's "wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct." The burden of proof is clear and convincing evidence (S.C. Code § 15-33-135). South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530), though the cap does not apply in cases involving DUI, felony conduct, or when the defendant acted with specific intent to harm.
after: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D), South Carolina allows punitive damages only where the plaintiff proves that the harm was the result of the defendant's "wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct." The burden of proof is clear and convincing evidence (S.C. Code § 15-33-135). South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530; the floor is indexed each year, $739,245 in 2026), though the cap does not apply when the defendant intended to harm the plaintiff and did, pled guilty to or was convicted of a felony arising from the same conduct, or acted while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (§ 15-32-530(C)).

When Gross Negligence Leads to Punitive Damages

Punitive damages are the primary financial consequence that separates gross negligence from ordinary negligence. While compensatory damages reimburse you for your actual losses, punitive damages are designed to punish the defendant and deter similar conduct in the future.
after:
Gross Negligence and Punitive Damages

Punitive damages are the primary financial consequence of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct, and gross negligence alone does not qualify in Georgia. While compensatory damages reimburse you for your actual losses, punitive damages are designed to punish the defendant and deter similar conduct in the future.

before: In both Georgia and South Carolina, punitive damages require proof by clear and convincing evidence — a higher standard than the "preponderance of the evidence" used for compensatory damages. This means you must show that it is highly probable that the defendant's conduct rose to the level of gross negligence, willful misconduct, or reckless disregard.
after: In both Georgia and South Carolina, punitive damages require proof by clear and convincing evidence — a higher standard than the "preponderance of the evidence" used for compensatory damages. This means you must show that it is highly probable that the defendant's conduct rose to the level of willful misconduct, wantonness, or reckless disregard.

before: Drunk driving cases represent one of the strongest categories for punitive damages. In Georgia, the $250,000 cap on punitive damages is removed entirely when the defendant was under the influence (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)(1)). This means DUI-related accident victims can seek unlimited punitive damages in Georgia. South Carolina similarly removes its punitive damages cap for DUI-related injuries, making these cases among the highest-value personal injury claims in both states.
after: Drunk driving cases represent one of the strongest categories for punitive damages. In Georgia, the $250,000 cap does not apply when the defendant's judgment was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)). There is no statutory cap on that award, though it can be recovered only from the impaired driver, not from other defendants. South Carolina similarly removes its cap where the defendant's judgment was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (S.C. Code § 15-32-530(C)(3)).

before: Ordinary negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care, while gross negligence involves conscious disregard for others' safety. Georgia recognizes three degrees of negligence under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-4 and caps punitive damages at $250,000 under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, except for DUI cases. South Carolina caps punitive damages at three times compensatory damages or $500,000 under S.C. Code § 15-32-530. Georgia's comparative fault threshold is 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina's is 51%.
after: Ordinary negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care, while gross negligence involves conscious disregard for others' safety. Georgia recognizes three degrees of negligence under O.C.G.A. §§ 51-1-2 through 51-1-4 (§ 51-1-4 defines gross negligence). In Georgia, negligence, even gross negligence, does not support punitive damages; O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b) requires clear and convincing evidence of wilful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression or conscious indifference. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, with no cap where the defendant intended harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs, or in product liability cases. South Carolina requires wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D)) and caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (indexed each year; $739,245 in 2026) under S.C. Code § 15-32-530. Georgia's comparative fault threshold is 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina's is 51% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.).

before: Yes. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, Georgia allows punitive damages when the defendant's conduct shows willful misconduct, malice, or conscious indifference to consequences. Punitive damages are capped at $250,000 in most cases, but the cap is removed for DUI-related accidents.
after: Not for gross negligence by itself. Georgia allows punitive damages only on clear and convincing evidence of willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression or an entire want of care showing conscious indifference to consequences (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b)); the Supreme Court of Georgia has held that negligence, even gross negligence, is not enough (Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown, 258 Ga. 115 (1988)). Where punitive damages are awarded they are capped at $250,000 in most cases, with no cap where the defendant intended harm or acted while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (§ 51-12-5.1(f)), or in product liability cases (§ 51-12-5.1(e)).

before: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000. The cap does not apply when the defendant was under the influence of alcohol or drugs, committed a felony, or acted with specific intent to harm.
after: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed for inflation each year ($739,245 in 2026). The cap does not apply when the defendant intended to harm the plaintiff and did, pled guilty to or was convicted of a felony arising from the same conduct, or acted while impaired by alcohol or drugs to the degree that their judgment was substantially impaired (§ 15-32-530(C)).

before: South Carolina is slightly more favorable. Georgia bars recovery if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), while South Carolina allows recovery as long as you are less than 51% at fault. A plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault can recover in South Carolina but not in Georgia.
after: South Carolina is slightly more favorable. Georgia bars recovery if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), while South Carolina allows recovery as long as you are less than 51% at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). A plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault can recover in South Carolina but not in Georgia.
